meta.source: Kumar, P. C., Subramaniam, M., Vitak, J., Clegg, T. L., & Chetty, M. (2020). Strengthening Children's Privacy Literacy through Contextual Integrity. Media and Communication, 8(4), 175-184. https://doi.org/10.17645/mac.v8i4.3236
meta.practice: Children's disclosure and management of device/account passwords across three contexts — family life, friendship, and education — where the appropriateness of the same flow (telling someone a password) varies with context and transmission principle
meta.practice_input: Children (roughly ages 5-17) manage passwords for devices (computers, Chromebooks, tablets, smartphones) and accounts (games, social media, school). A widespread pattern surrounds how these passwords flow: parents commonly require children to disclose their passwords while withholding their own; siblings tell, trade, or deduce each other's passwords; children sometimes share passwords with close friends they trust, with friends who can help them in a game, or with 'grownup friends' who need them, while refusing strangers and non-friends; and at school, teachers keep students' passwords written on index cards, schools assign guessable passwords such as birthdays or initials, and students are told never to share them, though a teacher may permit an exception. Adults typically instruct children with a blanket rule: don't tell anyone your password. Should this pattern of password disclosure and the rules around it continue as-is, be modified, or be rejected?
meta.annotator_notes: Multi-context case annotated per instruction: the family-life strand is the primary norm set (s5 entries 1-3); the friendship and education variations are recorded as additional s5 norms (entries 4-6) because the cross-context variation in norms governing the same flow is the paper's central analytic content — this is the corpus's best STEP-2/STEP-5 exemplar for context identification and norm variation across contexts. The schema's s2.nested_contexts field is used to hold friendship and education even though the paper treats the three contexts as parallel, not nested; s2.domain names only the primary (family) context. s7 is thin and borderline: the harms/benefits enumerated (privacy violations, reputational harm, misattributed blame, intimacy) are children's stated reasons that the authors analytically classify through CI, plus the authors' own moves (trust as the question the principles implicate; close peer relations as 'an important societal priority'; children's limited autonomy in the education context) — a second pass should confirm which entries count as source step-7 work versus s5 evidence. Normalization judgment calls: 'requirement' normalized to 'need' (the paper glosses it as 'disclosing a password because someone needs it'); the unnamed parental practice of requiring children to disclose passwords non-reciprocally normalized to mandatory/compulsion with explicit=false (arguably 'need' per Family H's 'she always needs to know my password'). The paper's own worked CI example (Friend 1/Friend 2 love-interest disclosure under coercion, Section 2.2 and Table 1) is a complete mini-traversal with a violation verdict, but concerns a different information flow, not passwords — excluded from this gold and noted in source_deviations. Second-pass fields: s7 factor checklist, s5 completeness codings (entrenched vs contested), s4 normalization choices.
source_deviations: The analysis is organized by context (Findings 4.1 family life, 4.2 friendship, 4.3 education) rather than by the 9-step heuristic; the step mapping here is annotator-imposed.

The authors report that they 'drew diagrams depicting the information flows involving passwords' and 'identified the parameters of information flows' during analysis, but the published text never states crisp (sender, recipient, subject, info-type, TP) tuples for the password flows — flows appear as fragmented interview examples — so s1 is marked absent even though Table 1 shows the tuple format for a non-password example.

No prima facie assessment (s6): the appropriateness determinations reported are the children's and parents' own per-flow perceptions ('parsed participants' determinations of appropriateness'); the authors never issue a norm-departure verdict on the practice.

No s9 verdict: the Discussion issues pedagogical recommendations — shift privacy literacy from rules to norms; reframe 'don't tell anyone your password' as 'only disclose your password to someone you trust'; use learning moments to discuss privacy norms with children; teach password lessons through non-education contexts (e.g., game accounts); accommodate developmental variation — these are recommendations about privacy education, not a continue/modify/reject decision on the disclosure practice itself.

Evaluative material is interleaved with descriptive material: children's harm/benefit reasons appear inside the friendship norm description (Section 4.2), and the step-8-style contextual-ends arguments (close peer relations as societal priority; teacher card-keeping and parental password knowledge 'make sense in context') appear in the Discussion (Section 5.1-5.2) inside the rules-to-norms pedagogical argument.

The paper's complete illustrative CI traversal (the Friend 1/Friend 2 love-interest example in Section 2.2, incl. coercion as TP and a violation pronouncement) concerns a different flow than the practice analyzed; the password analysis itself never reaches steps 6 or 9.

s2_context.domain: family life (children's and parents' management of passwords for shared and personal devices and accounts in the household)
nested_contexts: friendship (peer relationships among children; analyzed by the source as a parallel context with its own norms, not literally nested)
education (school; teachers, students, and classmates managing school-account passwords; also parallel)
research interview conducted in the family home (children disclosed passwords to interviewers, read by the source through mutuality or requirement)
activities: accessing shared and personal devices (computer, Chromebook, tablet, smartphone) and accounts (games, email, social media, school)
knowing, remembering, forgetting, discerning, and disclosing passwords
parents creating and storing passwords for children (e.g., written on paper kept 'in the coupon box')
backing up and re-downloading a device after a forgotten password
limiting children's time on devices (withholding passwords so children 'don't get into her computer when she's not looking')
play and transgression (nonchalantly creating accounts, cleverly deducing a sibling's password)
purposes: controlling access to devices and accounts (passwords 'require protection not because of what they mean but because of what they do—control access')
parental oversight and supervision of children's technology use
assisting children whose memory and developmental capacities are still evolving (avoiding lockouts and device resets)
keeping siblings and others out of one's device, account, or games
values_ends: trust between family members (and, in the parallel contexts, the trust that binds friendships)
parental care and responsibility for children ('Grounding privacy literacy in appropriate norms does not mean ceding responsibility for information flows to children')
children's developing privacy understanding and skill ('such experiences may also be necessary for children to learn privacy norms')
age-graded autonomy that grows as children gain experience in different social contexts
s2_context.evidence: Findings 4 intro (p. 178): 'Children's password management practices spanned three contexts: family life, friendship, and education. Children encountered passwords while accessing devices... and accounts'; Section 4.1 (pp. 178-179); Discussion 5.1-5.2 (pp. 180-181)

senders: children (disclosing their own passwords, or family passwords such as the family iPad password)
parents/caregivers (disclosing household or personal device passwords to children, conditionally or not at all)
siblings (telling, trading, or having passwords deduced from them)
teachers (distributing students' passwords written on cards)
recipients: parents/caregivers (who often required children to disclose any passwords they managed)
children (as conditional recipients of parents' or household passwords)
classmates and peers (incl. peeking while a password is typed)
interviewers (in-home researchers to whom some children disclosed passwords)
strangers/non-friends (hypothetical recipients whom children deemed inappropriate)
subjects: the child who owns the password-protected account or device (the paper treats the password as belonging/referring to its holder, per Table 1's 'information subject... to whom the information belongs or refers')
parents (their own device passwords, e.g., a mother's phone passcode or Kindle password)
the family collectively (the family iPad password)
indirectly, friends and family whose 'personal family business' is reachable through the account behind the password

nonhuman_roles.entity: devices and accounts (computer, Chromebook, tablet, smartphone; game, social media, and school accounts)
written password artifacts (index cards kept by teachers or in desks; paper slips in the coupon box)
school/district password-assignment schemes (birthdays, initials, six-digit issuance)

s3_actors.evidence: Sections 4.1-4.3 (pp. 178-180): 'The family life context encompassed password practices among parents, children, and siblings'; 'Discussions about password sharing among friends or generic other people'; 'The education context encompassed password practices among teachers, students, and classmates'; Family G quote on personal family business (p. 179)

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: secrecy ('don't tell anyone your password' ascribes secrecy to the password)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 5.1 (p. 180): 'Rules like don't tell anyone your password ascribe secrecy to the password... In CI terms, secrecy equals the stoppage of information flows, but children did not experience passwords as secret'; Section 4.2: 'Children were usually told not to disclose passwords to others, with secrecy or confidentiality as the underlying transmission principle'; Section 4.2 (Family V): 'returning to the transmission principle of secrecy'; Section 4.3: a 6-year-old called his school password 'secret' (Family X)

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: confidentiality (only a (grand)parent or teacher should know a password)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 5.1 (p. 180): 'A more fitting transmission principle is confidentiality, which "focuses on relationships" and "involves trusting others to refrain from revealing personal information to unauthorized individuals" (Richards & Solove, 2007, p. 125). Rules like don't tell anyone except a parent or teacher your password imply confidentiality'; Section 4.1 (Family 12): 'before reverting to one of confidentiality—that only a (grand)parent or teacher should know a password'

Section 4.1 (p. 178), Family 12 grandmother ('You don't tell your passwords ever, to any of those, unless you tell meemaw'): 'In CI terms, this caregiver suggested a transmission principle of notice—telling the grandparent—before reverting to one of confidentiality'

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: requirement (disclosing a password because someone needs it)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 5.1 (p. 180): 'requirement (disclosing a password because someone needs it)'; Section 4.2 (Family F, the 'grownup friend... because she needed [the password]'): 'Here, the transmission principle of requirement superseded that of confidentiality'; Section 4.1 (Family S): 'or of requirement, treating the interviewer as an authority figure whose presence in his home demanded knowledge of the password'

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: exchange (each party benefits from the information flow)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 4.2 (p. 179), Family B: 'An 11-year-old said he felt comfortable sharing game passwords with friends if doing so could help him in the game, invoking the transmission principle of exchange—each party benefits from the information flow'; Section 5.1: 'exchange (disclosing because you'll receive something in return)'

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: mutuality (disclosing as a form of relational intimacy)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 4.2 (p. 179), Family Y ('my really close friend who I trust, I just tell her my password and she tells me her password'): 'This girl invoked the transmission principle of mutuality, evaluating the appropriateness of the flow in part based on whether she trusted the recipient'; Section 4.1 (Family S): 'the transmission principle of mutuality, treating the interviewer as a friend whom he could trust with the password'; Section 5.1: 'mutuality (disclosing as a form of relational intimacy)'

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: consent (the password can be disclosed if the teacher permits the student to do so)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 4.3 (p. 180), Family C (teacher allowed a 6-year-old to share her password with a classmate who lacked an account): 'Here, we see the transmission principle shift from secrecy, suggesting the password should not be disclosed at all, to one of consent, where the password can be disclosed if the teacher permits the student to do so'

s4_transmission_principles.source_label: parents required children to disclose any passwords they managed (not named as a TP by the authors)
s4_transmission_principles.evidence: Section 4.1 (p. 178): 'Passwords did not flow reciprocally between parents and children; while parents could withhold passwords from children, they often required children to disclose any passwords they managed to parents'; Family H: 'My mom knows my password, and that's the first person I need to tell because she always needs to know my password'

s5_norms.norm_flow: FAMILY (primary): Children (senders/subjects) disclose their device and account passwords (information type) to parents (recipients) on parental demand; the flow is non-reciprocal and compulsory (TPs: mandatory/compulsion, need) — parents are entitled to know children's passwords, children are not entitled to parents'
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'Passwords did not flow reciprocally between parents and children; while parents could withhold passwords from children, they often required children to disclose any passwords they managed to parents'; children internalize it ('My mom knows my password, and that's the first person I need to tell', Family H); parents create and store children's passwords ('My mom usually makes a password for me and puts it on a piece of paper', Family G); grounded in caregiving ('Parents may want to know a child's password so they do not have to reset a device if/when the child forgets it', Section 5.2)
departures: a 7-year-old would not want her mother to know her tablet's password 'because I don't want my mom getting on my iPad and seeing what my future birthday presents [are]' (Family D)
some children expressed interest in keeping their parents out of their devices

s5_norms.norm_flow: FAMILY (primary): Parents (senders/subjects) disclose household or their own device passwords to children (recipients) conditionally — under confidentiality (tell no one else) or notice — or refuse entirely, because parents do not uniformly regard children as appropriate password recipients
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: A mother refused to disclose a password so her kids 'don't get into her computer when she's not looking' (Family C); 'Oh please don't, you'll lock both of us out if you do that' (Family D); 'Other children said parents told them passwords on the condition that they not tell others'; the Family 12 grandmother's notice-then-confidentiality rule; 'Families understandably differed in their beliefs about what constituted an appropriate recipient of a password... influenced in part by children's abilities and dispositions relating to, for instance, remembering a password or limiting their time spent playing computer games'
departures: a 6-year-old said she tried to get her mother to reveal her phone's passcode 'so when she's like, in the shower, I can get onto it' (Family K)
a 7-year-old said she was going to try and figure out her mother's Kindle password (Family D)
a 5-year-old disclosed his family's iPad password to the interviewer despite his mother's key-guarding rule (Family S)

s5_norms.norm_flow: FAMILY (primary): Password flows between siblings (senders/recipients/subjects: siblings) are variable and negotiated — some siblings tell each other passwords, others withhold them, and deducing a sibling's password is a live move within play and transgression
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'Password flows also varied between siblings. An 11-year-old said she told her 8-year-old sister her email password (Family V). Others deduced siblings' passwords or vice-versa'; a 9-year-old 'figured out my brother's password on his phone' via the phone number and was rewarded with a bargain ('if you figure out the password then I'll let you play on it', Family 7); 'Password management also involved play and transgression... These are typical aspects of child behavior... such experiences may also be necessary for children to learn privacy norms (Wolfe & Laufer, 1975)'
departures: targeted siblings defend the norm boundary: an 11-year-old changed his phone's password from four to six digits after his 8-year-old brother figured it out, and later changed it again when the younger boy overheard the new one (Family B)
the targeted sibling may feel annoyed or concerned that the perpetrating sibling might mess up their device or account

s5_norms.norm_flow: FRIENDSHIP (cross-context variation): The default norm children are taught — do not disclose passwords to others (TPs: secrecy/confidentiality) — is superseded among friends by relationship-sensitive principles: mutuality with a close trusted friend, exchange when both parties benefit in a game, need when a 'grownup friend' requires it; appropriateness of the same flow depends on the friend and the trust invested
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'Children were usually told not to disclose passwords to others, with secrecy or confidentiality as the underlying transmission principle'; the Family Y 10-year-old's mutuality reasoning ('If it's someone that you don't know very well... I wouldn't do it. But... [she's] my really close friend who I trust, I just tell her my password and she tells me her password... I know that she's not going to tell anyone else because I trust her'); the Family B exchange case; the Family F requirement case; 'children also acknowledged that disclosing passwords with friends could yield benefits or reinforce intimacy (Marwick & boyd, 2014)'
departures: 'Some participants said children should only disclose passwords to parents, while others mentioned that children may not want to reveal passwords to anyone' — the friend-disclosure norm is openly disputed among families
disclosing to a friend risks 'someone telling others the password, looking at personal accounts, or doing something on the device or account that could get the child in trouble'

s5_norms.norm_flow: FRIENDSHIP/NON-FRIENDS (cross-context variation): Children do not disclose passwords to non-friends or strangers — an unqualified prohibition children themselves endorse (TP: secrecy)
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'Indeed, when the conversation turned to disclosing passwords to non-friends, children deemed such flows inappropriate'; 'I don't like people messing up my games' (Family B); the Animal Jam 6-year-old ('if they steal your phone... They could do bad stuff on it', Family N); the Family G 8-year-old ('It's my personal business, not theirs... I might get in trouble for something I didn't do'); the Family P stranger scenario ('maybe they could post something bad [about] our friends')

s5_norms.norm_flow: EDUCATION (cross-context variation): School passwords flow within an institutional regime — teachers keep and distribute students' passwords (written on index cards, 'for safekeeping'), schools assign guessable passwords (birthdays, initials) and offer optional changes, and students are prohibited from sharing school passwords (TP: secrecy) except when the teacher permits disclosure (TP: consent)
s5_norms.entrenchment_evidence: 'Children said teachers gave students their passwords, often written on a card... his teacher kept the cards for safekeeping' (Family A); 'several children said they were not allowed to share school passwords'; the teacher-permitted exception (Family C); schools using birthdays/initials as passwords with change optional (Families Q, I, 13, W); Section 5.2: 'Teachers may write student passwords on index cards because helping children reset their passwords if/when they forget them consumes valuable instruction time. Practices that seem to contradict general privacy and security advice make sense in context'
departures: classmates peek at passwords being typed ('they're supposed to cover [it with] their hand...and not look....I type my...passcode in fast so [classmates] won't know, but then they still know it because they peek at it', Family C)
students 'type random numbers and then get into someone's account' — the penguin-to-bicycle profile-image incident, met with a 'no hacking' announcement but no required password change (Family B)
passwords could be inferred: a 7-year-old's initials served as her math-game password, 'meaning classmates knew each other's passwords' (Family Q)

children themselves did not find flows of their school information problematic ('you don't really get to any of our private information by a Chromebook', Family G; 'everybody in my class has the same [information on their Chromebooks]', Family C)
some school password practices went against security best practices (Section 5.2)

s7_factors.factor: Trust is what the password-governing transmission principles implicate: 'do you trust this person needs the password? Do you trust that disclosing a password will yield the promised benefit? Do you trust that your friend won't mess up your account?' — trust both licenses appropriate disclosure and is what betrayal damages
s7_factors.evidence: Section 5.1 (pp. 180-181): 'These principles implicate trust, raising questions like...'; the proposed reframed rule: 'don't tell anyone your password becomes only disclose your password to someone you trust'; Section 2.2 (p. 176-177, framing): coerced disclosure 'rattles the trust that binds friendships'

s7_factors.factor: Disclosure to the wrong recipient yields reputational harm and misattributed blame: 'someone posting negative content about you' and 'getting in trouble (if the person does something bad or inappropriate while using your accounts)'
s7_factors.evidence: Section 4.2 (p. 179): 'Children said disclosing passwords to non-friends could result in... reputational harm (someone posting negative content about you), and getting in trouble'; Family G: 'maybe they would use it for something that I didn't do and I might get in trouble for something I didn't do'; Family P: 'they could post something bad [about] our friends and then our friends wouldn't like us anymore just because of them'

s7_factors.factor: Privacy violations through onward exposure: a password is a gateway, so its disclosure exposes personal and family information behind it ('someone seeing information you don't want them to see'; 'my password may be connected to any of my personal family business')
s7_factors.evidence: Section 4.2 (p. 179): 'privacy violations (someone seeing information you don't want them to see)'; Family G: 'If that password may be connected to any of my personal family business or any of my business, then I don't want anyone to be looking into it and finding out any of my own stuff'

s7_factors.factor: Password disclosure among friends can 'yield benefits or reinforce intimacy' — mutual disclosure is a form of relational intimacy supporting close relations between peers, which the authors call 'an important societal priority'
s7_factors.evidence: Section 4.2 (p. 179): 'children also acknowledged that disclosing passwords with friends could yield benefits or reinforce intimacy (Marwick & boyd, 2014)'; Section 5.1 (p. 181): 'this flow could be appropriate because it supports close relations between peers, an important societal priority'

s7_factors.factor: Children's limited autonomy in the education context: 'Children are required to go to school, follow the schedules set out for them, complete the tasks assigned to them, and submit their work for evaluation. Younger children in particular experience little autonomy over the information on their Chromebooks'
s7_factors.evidence: Section 4.3 (p. 180): the authors use this structural autonomy deficit to explain why children 'may find it appropriate for that information to flow to others, even if it sits behind a password'

s7_factors.factor: Parent-child power asymmetry: password flows are non-reciprocal (parents may withhold and compel), which the authors treat as legitimate parental responsibility rather than a wrong — 'grounding privacy literacy in appropriate norms does not mean ceding responsibility for information flows to children'
s7_factors.evidence: Section 4.1 (p. 178): 'Passwords did not flow reciprocally between parents and children'; Section 5.2 (p. 181): 'Parents may want to know a child's password so they do not have to reset a device if/when the child forgets it'

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: close relations between peers — the defining end of the friendship context
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: 'A few children expressed comfort telling a close friend a password. In CI terms, this flow could be appropriate because it supports close relations between peers, an important societal priority.' Mutuality-governed password disclosure advances the friendship context's ends, which is why the blanket secrecy rule ('don't tell anyone your password') misdescribes the context: the flow's appropriateness turns on the trust between the parties, not on stopping the flow. Hence the authors' proposed norm-sensitive replacement, 'only disclose your password to someone you trust.'

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: efficient instruction and the completion and evaluation of students' work — the ends of the education context
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: Practices that violate general security advice serve education's contextual ends: 'Teachers may write student passwords on index cards because helping children reset their passwords if/when they forget them consumes valuable instruction time. Practices that seem to contradict general privacy and security advice make sense in context.' And because schooling is compulsory and children have little autonomy over their Chromebook information, the flows behind school passwords carry little contextual weight for children — which the authors use to explain why children did not question those flows and why password lessons would resonate more if taught through non-education contexts such as a game account.

s8_contextual_meaning.contextual_end: parental care and oversight of children — the ends of the family-life context
s8_contextual_meaning.argument: The compulsory, non-reciprocal child-to-parent password flow advances the family context's caregiving ends: 'Parents may want to know a child's password so they do not have to reset a device if/when the child forgets it.' The authors argue such context-fit — rather than compliance with generic rules — is what privacy literacy should teach, 'particularly when considering children's evolving cognitive, social, and emotional development.'
